newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rejects report it obtained secret U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Israel rejects report it obtained secret U.S. data.

text.p: Israel denied on Wednesday a Washington Post report the FBI was probing whether a senior U.S. government official had been passing highly sensitive information to the Israeli government.
"There is not a shred of truth to it. It is simply a fabrication," an aide of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said of the Post report published on Wednesday.

Quoting sources with direct knowledge of the inquiry, the newspaper said the investigation was launched in January after the National Security Agency intercepted a secure communication between a senior Israeli intelligence officer in Washington and a superior in Tel Aviv.

The communication referred to someone codenamed "Mega" and an attempt to obtain a sensitive American document, according to the report. The Post said U.S. officials believed Mega may be someone in the U.S. government who provided information to the Israelis in the past.

"Israel does not do things of this nature," Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told reporters. "Our diplomats throughout the world, and in particular in the United States, of course, do not deal in things like this. They have clear instructions."

The United States is Israel's main ally. Relations between the two countries were strained 12 years ago when a Jewish U.S. naval intelligence officer was caught passing information to Israel. The officer, Jonathan Pollard, pleaded guilty to spying charges in 1986 and has since been serving a life sentence.

The Post's sources said the new investigation was focusing on U.S. officials who would have had access to the document in question, a secret letter of assurances given by then Secretary of State Warren Christopher to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat after successful negotiations to withdraw Israeli troops from most of the West Bank city of Hebron.
Netanyahu's media adviser David Bar-Illan told Israel Radio: "We are unfortunately aware of such fabrications that are sometimes created by certain parties who are not particularly friendly to us."

In the intercepted conversation, according to two unidentified U.S. officials quoted by the Post, the Israeli intelligence officer informed his superior in Tel Aviv that Israeli Ambassador Eliahu Ben Elissar had asked him whether he could obtain a copy of the letter Christopher gave to Arafat on Jan. 16, the day after the Hebron accord was signed.
Ben-Elissar told Israel Radio: "It is first-class nonsense, one of those things that falls on us probably from a sick imagination."

He added: "Israel does not collect intelligence in the U.S. and this is a terrible report whose purpose is to accuse Israel of spying against the U.S. This is unimaginable and terribly severe. We do not spy in the U.S."
